name: Ivan Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What fills a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and repair overhead power lines for the electricity company, mostly older poles and transformers along the river road. I earned a vocational certificate through an apprenticeship and know the odd old fittings, even if I'm an ordinary crew hand rather than a lead. I still like the moment lights come on, but my shoulders ache after a long bucket day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and how much AI do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a pharmacy counter, and our two children are grown and living their own lives. We have around four months of expenses saved, typical lineworker pay and a few other crews within reach; retirement is in sight but we haven't fixed the date. I use AI every day to turn spoken job notes into reports, then correct the part names myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot my voice-to-text notes still save me ten minutes after a repair. The old poles and transformers still need someone out there with tools, so the grand AI talk can cool down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is a comfortable picture for my remaining working years. My partner's pharmacy counter job and my line pay cover our bills, and we have around four months of expenses set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the overhead repair shifts and using AI to turn my spoken notes into reports. At the end of each job I'll compare the report's part numbers with the actual tags before sending it to stores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a hint of disappointment because I like trying new tools. A steady few years would be easy on our household planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did your note app get a repair wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the app heard 'fuse link' as 'fuel line' after a windy callout. I corrected the part name before the stores team sent anything, which was easier than rewriting the whole job report. My AI report heard 'fuse link' as 'fuel line'; the stores team needed the real part number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a quieter future change your retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't move the retirement date just because a form is easier. I will review our income and savings with my partner each year, then decide when leaving work is affordable.

say: **Spoken reports** can save time, but lineworkers still repair poles and transformers.
A **parts check** still belongs with the worker who saw the damaged hardware.
think: My **line income** and my partner's pharmacy work look steady for now.
Our **four-month reserve** gives us space to plan the final working years.
do: **Keep** overhead repair shifts and use the existing voice-to-text report tool.
**Compare** reported part numbers with equipment tags before ordering.
feel: **Calm** about income, a little disappointed that tools may remain modest.
S0.quote: My AI report heard 'fuse link' as 'fuel line'; the stores team needed the real part number.
fieldNote: He likes **AI convenience** but catches a concrete error before parts are ordered.
The retirement date stays **undecided** pending household financial reviews, not a guaranteed age.

steps.text: Keep overhead repair shifts and current voice report tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying and booking may be handed to software, while a robot will take longer to replace a transformer beside a road. I'd ask who checks the order when the system guesses the wrong fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn a new planner, but I doubt it would change most of my repair hours soon. If office staff are cut, the depot might make field crews correct more orders after a long shift without paying for the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll test the approved parts planner on three completed transformer jobs and compare its list with what we actually used. If it performs well, I'll learn its corrections on company time and record any extra checking minutes on our job sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the workload, not about a lost wage tomorrow. I have enough room to complain constructively before it becomes the new normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a missing connector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the missing connector and refuse the order until stores confirm the right one. My crew driving back from a roadside power transformer for one missing connector would cost more than checking the AI order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show the new work takes time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the checking minutes beside the old job times and take both to the supervisor. If the new planner saves the office an hour but takes our crew thirty minutes, I want that visible.

say: **Parts planners** may speed office buying, but transformer fittings still need a worker's check.
**Robots** will reach roadside repairs more slowly than AI reaches booking and ordering.
think: My **repair shifts** look fairly safe in the slower change.
More **order checking** could land on field crews after long shifts.
do: **Test** the approved planner against three completed transformer jobs.
**Learn** its correction controls on paid time if the three-job test succeeds.
feel: **Uneasy** about unpaid checking, while expecting regular repair wages.
S1.quote: My crew driving back from a roadside power transformer for one missing connector would cost more than checking the AI order.
fieldNote: He accepts software after a **three-job comparison**, which fits his curiosity and practical trade experience.
His worry is **extra checking time** rather than direct job loss.

steps.text: Test approved AI planner on three completed transformer jobs
Learn planner corrections on paid time if three-job test succeeds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 changes dispatch and orders first. Capable repair robots around 2031 arrive when I'll be about 63, so the company should tell older lineworkers which paid shifts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months of bills in savings would not bridge years without my wage. I might be close to retirement by 2031, but I have not checked the numbers closely enough to promise we can live on it then. Four months of savings cannot bridge years between a lineworker layoff and an affordable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the employer for its 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing plans. I'll book a retirement-income meeting with the plan administrator and take a paid robot inspection trial and learn its controls if one is offered while I keep my line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious; I can make calls, but I cannot turn a guess about retirement money into a mortgage payment. A cut in repair shifts before I am ready to stop would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner and grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner I want the actual figures before we change our spending. I would tell our grown children we are looking at options, not asking them for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which retirement figures would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the administrator to show what our monthly income would be if my shifts ended at 63 and if I worked longer. Until I have those figures, I am not moving the retirement date or quitting the crew.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before capable field robots arrive around 2031.
The company should publish **paid repair shifts** for older lineworkers before making promises.
think: A robot could cut my **line hours** near 63, before I know whether retirement is affordable.
Our **four-month savings** cannot replace years of a full wage.
do: **Ask** employer for 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing plans.
**Book** a retirement-income review covering a 63-year exit and longer work.
**Use** robot inspection controls in a paid trial if offered while keeping line shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss before a financially workable retirement.
S2.quote: Four months of savings cannot bridge years between a lineworker layoff and an affordable retirement.
fieldNote: He asks for **actual retirement figures**, without treating the enquiry as early retirement.
The trial is conditional on **paid time** and keeping his line shifts.
His 2031 concern is **robot exposure at 63**, not immediate replacement by thinking AI.

steps.text: Ask employer for 2028 dispatch and 2031 field plans
Book retirement-income review comparing exit at 63 with longer work
Use robot inspection controls in paid trial if offered while keeping shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 still changes the office first, but field robots around 2034 would meet me closer to the age when I hope to stop climbing. Five years is enough to settle the money question rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stay on repairs for a while if my shoulders hold. A paid fault-checking post might make those last years easier, but I will not assume the company has one waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll review our retirement income and household costs each year, and add a small extra debt payment from each wage while both of us are working. If the company posts a paid fault-checker vacancy with lighter field duties, I'll apply and compare its wage with my repair pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but five years gives me room to calculate and adjust. I would like my last working years to be planned, not pushed by a machine announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why might lighter field work matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shoulders complain after two long bucket days, so a real checker role could matter even without robots. A real power-line fault-checker job could spare my shoulders without taking away the wage that pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra mortgage payment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra payment would come from dropping our monthly paid television package, then sending that amount from each new wage toward the mortgage. If pharmacy hours fall, we'd keep the normal payment instead.

say: **2031 thinking AI** reaches office tasks before repair robots arrive around 2034.
A **five-year runway** lets older workers calculate whether a later move or retirement is affordable.
think: My **shoulders** may make lighter paid field work useful before I stop working.
A **checker vacancy** could help, but no employer has offered one.
do: **Review** retirement income and household costs every year.
**Overpay** the mortgage from cancelled television spending while both wages continue.
**Apply** for paid fault-checker vacancy if duties are lighter and wages cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about later shifts, with time to make financial choices.
S3.quote: A real power-line fault-checker job could spare my shoulders without taking away the wage that pays our bills.
fieldNote: He considers lighter work for **shoulder strain** as well as potential robots.
Extra mortgage payments are **new debt payments** from wages, conditional on both incomes.
The checker plan depends on a **paid vacancy** with adequate wages and lighter duties.

steps.text: Review retirement income and household costs annually
Overpay mortgage from cancelled television cost while both wages continue
Apply for paid lighter fault-checker vacancy if wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI in 2036 and field robots around 2039 are far enough out that I would expect to have stopped regular climbing by then, if our finances allow it. I would still want younger crews trained to check the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the field robot date I'd be about 71, so the main issue is whether our own retirement plan works before then. I cannot promise an exit year today, but the longer timetable makes this technology less threatening to my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll sit down with my partner and our retirement statements, then set a savings target from future pay for the years after work. I'll continue the repair rota while it suits my body and check the plan each year before choosing a final date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the technology timetable, though money still deserves a careful look. I like having the option to leave on our terms. A line-repair robot arriving when I am about 71 is less frightening than a retirement budget that does not add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown son about the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown son to learn how to test a line even if a robot might one day lift the fitting. I will be glad to leave him a trade with a proper safety habit, not just a button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you that stopping work is affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would only stop climbing when the monthly retirement figures cover our ordinary bills and a cushion for repairs. If they do not, I will keep earning and review the date again.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and 2039 field robots give me time to decide when climbing can end.
**Young crews** still need line testing skills even if machines later lift fittings.
think: At about **71** when field robots arrive, I expect to be off regular climbs if finances allow.
Our **retirement numbers** must cover bills before I set a final work exit date.
do: **Review** retirement statements with my partner this year and annually after.
**Save** a set amount from future wages toward years after linework.
feel: **Calm** about the technology timetable, attentive to retirement finances.
S4.quote: A line-repair robot arriving when I am about 71 is less frightening than a retirement budget that does not add up.
fieldNote: He plans around **finances**, without inventing a guaranteed statutory pension age.
The 2039 field robot date lands **beyond climbing**, subject to the household budget being affordable.

steps.text: Review retirement statements with partner this year and annually
Save set amount from future wages for years after linework

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because repair robots could reach my crew around 2031, before I know whether stopping work at about 63 is affordable. A staffing plan and real retirement-income figures would let us choose rather than guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company will keep paid work for older lineworkers who know the old fittings but cannot climb every day. I want the numbers, not a farewell speech. A report app gives my lineworker shoulders a break after a shift; a proper lighter job could help before retirement.

headlineQuote: A report app gives my lineworker shoulders a break after a shift; a proper lighter job could help before retirement.
portrait: **Ivan**, 58, repairs older power lines after a vocational certificate and apprenticeship, with retirement in sight but no fixed date.
He uses **AI daily** for spoken repair notes and checks its part names against the equipment.
His **four-month savings**, typical pay and pharmacy-counter partner support a careful transition, while shoulder pain limits long bucket shifts.
Fast field robots make him **anxious** about a wage gap; a longer runway lets him calculate retirement and seek lighter paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring field robots around 2031 before an affordable retirement date is clear.
whatWouldHelp: A **crew staffing plan** and actual retirement-income figures would help him decide how long to keep working.
